clue.text: A health-giving double?

parts.note: a toast drinks someone's health, and this toast is one short word said twice over, a doubled word

explanation.surface: A tonic or a second helping that does you good.
explanation.walkthrough: The toast 'chin-chin' wishes the hearer good health, so it is 'health-giving', and it is the word CHIN doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: Chin-chin is an old-fashioned drinking toast, a salute to someone's health as glasses are raised.

clue.text: Pitcher got down to battle in 1797

definitions.text: Pitcher got down to battle in 1797

parts.words: Pitcher got down to battle in 1797
parts.note: a pitcher is one who pitches a tent; add the word 'down' and you have the name of Admiral Duncan's 1797 victory over the Dutch fleet

explanation.surface: A baseball pitcher squared up for a fight in the eighteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' suggests a jug or a ballplayer, but here it is someone who pitches a tent. That word with DOWN after it names the Battle of Camperdown, fought off the Dutch coast in 1797.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pitches a tent and sleeps under canvas is a holidaymaker of the outdoor kind.

clue.text: No place for those who would get on top

definitions.text: No place for those who would get on top

parts.words: No place for those who would get on top
parts.note: on an old double-decker bus, passengers who want the upper deck do not stay in the lower saloon

explanation.surface: A warning to the ambitious that this is no place for climbers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about getting ahead in life; the clue means the lower deck of a bus or coach, where those wanting to ride 'on top' would not sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The enclosed lower part of a double-decker bus, as opposed to the open top deck, is the interior seating.

clue.text: Sweet heliotrope

definitions.meaning: a sweet is a pudding, here one of fruit baked in pastry
a garden plant with fragrant purple flowers whose cottage name is the same as the pudding

explanation.surface: A sweet-smelling purple flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective for the flower, but it is the British word for a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastry dessert filled with red stone fruit, and also an old country name for the heliotrope plant, whose flowers smell of it.

clue.text: You must bear life's fun badly if you find it so

definitions.text: You must bear life's fun badly if you find it so

indicators.note: something done badly is botched and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the possessive s counts here as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: Only a miserable person would find life's fun unbearable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges BEAR LIFES FUN; the whole clue also defines: you take life's fun badly if you find it unbearable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something you cannot endure or tolerate is unbearable, so you would put up with it poorly.

clue.text: Knock on wood-this does. Keep it up !

definitions.meaning: a woodpecker taps on trees; the clue's 'wood-' joins to the answer to name the bird
the British idiom 'keep your ... up' means stay cheerful

explanation.surface: Touch wood for luck, and don't lose heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock on wood' looks like the superstitious phrase, but read with the hyphen 'wood-' plus the answer is the bird that knocks on wood. 'Keep your pecker up' is British slang for keep your spirits up.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird's beak is what does the tapping on trees, and courage or spirit is what you keep up in the idiom.

clue.text: Condemn to the fate of the Baskerville villain

definitions.text: Condemn to the fate of the Baskerville villain

parts.words: Condemn to the fate of the Baskerville villain
parts.note: in Conan Doyle's The Hound of the Baskervilles, the villain Stapleton is last seen fleeing into the Grimpen Mire and is presumed sunk in it

explanation.surface: Sentence someone to the end met by the wrongdoer in a Sherlock Holmes story.
explanation.walkthrough: The villain of The Hound of the Baskervilles, Stapleton, vanishes into the Grimpen Mire, a marsh on Dartmoor, so to share his fate is to be sunk in a mire.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink or plunge someone into a marsh or mire is to trap them in wet, swampy ground.

clue.text: It's not metal, which is in good order, that's creating hitches

indicators.note: the phrase 'which is in' puts the first pair of words inside the order's letters

parts.note: KG stands for Knight of the Garter, the most senior British order of chivalry
taken as written
tin is a metal

explanation.surface: Something that is not metal, and in fine condition, is causing snags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good order' sounds like tidiness, but it is the Order of the Garter, whose knights are KG; NOT TIN goes inside. 'Hitches' are knots tied in rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitch is a kind of knot, so tying hitches is tying a rope into loops and ties.

clue.text: The old thing begs for new coats

parts.note: res is the Latin word for a thing, the 'old' language here
to pray for something is to beg for it

explanation.surface: An elderly person pleads for some new clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old thing' looks like a person, but it is Latin res, thing. 'coats' are coats of paint, not garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh coats of paint applied to a car or surface are further sprayings over the old finish.

clue.text: She is sure to cause friction at work

definitions.text: She is sure to cause friction at work

parts.words: She is sure to cause friction at work
parts.note: a woman whose job is rubbing clients' muscles creates friction literally as she works

explanation.surface: A colleague who is bound to stir up trouble in the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'friction' suggests office quarrels, but here it is the literal rubbing of a woman who gives massages.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who massages people professionally rubs and kneads their muscles, which is friction in its physical sense.

clue.text: Is horrified by a cabhorse coming out of church !

indicators.note: the church's letters leave the long word, so they are removed from it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone is appalled by a horse emerging from a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming out of' takes C and E (CE, the Church of England) out of CABHORSE, leaving the rest in order.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe or detest something is to be revolted and horrified by it.

clue.text: This form of change has met much resistance

definitions.text: This form of change has met much resistance

parts.words: This form of change has met much resistance
parts.note: change means coins; the seven-sided fifty-pence piece introduced in 1969 drew many complaints from the British public

explanation.surface: A reform that has faced a lot of opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' suggests reform, but it is loose coins. Britain's seven-sided 50p coin of 1969 was widely disliked when it appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: A shape with seven sides, like the heptagonal British fifty-pence coin, has a seven-sided outline.

clue.text: One of the Brethren takes root

definitions.text: One of the Brethren takes root

parts.words: One of the Brethren takes root
parts.note: a senior officer of a church congregation such as the Brethren settles in, and the shrub of the same name strikes from cuttings readily

explanation.surface: A member of a religious community settles down.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a church official becoming established; the same word names a hedgerow shrub, the kind of thing that literally takes root.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior lay officer in Presbyterian and Brethren churches shares a name with Sambucus, a shrub grown in hedgerows.

clue.text: She has a free right, oddly enough, to hold goods for others

definitions.note: ships are traditionally referred to as she

indicators.note: something happening oddly is out of the usual pattern, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman has the free right to look after other people's possessions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges FREE RIGHT. 'She' is the ship, and 'to hold goods for others' describes the vessel's job.
explanation.definitionFit: A cargo ship is a vessel, conventionally feminine, built to carry goods for others.

clue.text: The lolly's lovely-but expensive

parts.note: lolly is British slang for money, lovely suggests pretty, and a large sum of money is an expensive amount

explanation.surface: An ice lolly that tastes delicious but costs a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lolly' looks like an ice lolly but is British slang for money; lovely money, a 'pretty' coin, is also a large sum.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a large sum of money: something that costs a lot is said to cost this much.

clue.text: Inclinations to write church music?

parts.note: to pen is to write
chants are sung in church services

explanation.surface: A wish to compose music for the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Inclinations are fondnesses or likings for something, strong tastes for it.

clue.text: Secret of the mysterious ice-store

indicators.note: something mysterious is puzzling and obscure, so these letters are shuffled into another order

explanation.surface: The hidden truth about a strange cold store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mysterious' rearranges ICESTORE, the letters of 'ice-store' without the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowledge understood only by a small inner circle is obscure and private, kept from outsiders.

clue.text: Party goes to the country-it's a gift!

parts.note: a do is a party
a nation is a country

explanation.surface: A political party takes over a country, and everyone thinks it a present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests politics, but it is a DO, a social gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given freely to a charity or cause is a present or contribution.

clue.text: Play not making much of a hit?

definitions.text: Play not making much of a hit?

parts.words: Play not making much of a hit?
parts.note: in cricket, a batsman who blocks every ball and scores slowly plays without hitting out

explanation.surface: A theatre production that has flopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' suggests a stage show and 'hit' a success, but this is cricket: stonewalling is dour defensive batting that scores few runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Defensive batting in cricket that blocks rather than scores, and by extension any obstructive delaying tactic.

clue.text: Statesman's son?

parts.note: a son sharing his father's name is marked Jr, as with American political dynasties

explanation.surface: Is this the politician's boy?
explanation.walkthrough: A son named after his statesman father is styled Jr after his name; the question mark flags the indirect definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A son with the same name as his father is distinguished by this title, meaning the younger one.

clue.text: " Their sober never learned to stray "(Gray)

definitions.text: " Their sober never learned to stray "(Gray)

parts.words: " Their sober never learned to stray "(Gray)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, describing the humble villagers' quiet desires

explanation.surface: A line of poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word in Thomas Gray's Elegy line 'Their sober wishes never learn'd to stray', about country folk content with simple hopes.
explanation.definitionFit: The villagers' desires or hopes are what the poet says never wandered beyond their modest lot.

clue.text: I tell you plainly, it's on the level

definitions.meaning: a blunt phrase ending an argument, meaning 'and that is final'
read literally, it says something is level or even

explanation.surface: I'm being frank with you: it's honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the level' looks like 'honest', but the second reading is literal: something lying perfectly even.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic refusal, 'and that is final', and read literally says a surface is level and even.

clue.text: Describing the conduct of one who would soak us so ?

definitions.text: Describing the conduct of one who would soak us so ?

parts.words: Describing the conduct of one who would soak us so ?
parts.note: to soak someone is to overcharge them, and an excessive price is described with a word that also means to soak in liquid

explanation.surface: How to describe someone who would drench us like that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soak' is slang for overcharging, and a price that soaks us is excessive; the same word as a verb means to soak something in liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessively high prices are called this, and the same word as a verb means to immerse or marinate.

clue.text: She helps us to cherish our ideals of beautiful womanhood

definitions.text: She helps us to cherish our ideals of beautiful womanhood

indicators.note: the clue's letters help us to the answer, which is lodged across the words that follow

explanation.surface: A woman who keeps our dreams of feminine beauty alive.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'cherisH OUR Ideals'; the whole clue also describes a nymph of the Muslim paradise, an ideal of female beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: In Islamic tradition, a beautiful maiden of paradise, and by extension any alluring young woman.

clue.text: The right helper proves incursive

definitions.note: the definition is an adjective describing one who makes incursions, while the answer is the noun for that person

parts.note: an aider is one who helps

explanation.surface: The correct assistant turns out to be invasive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incursive' means making incursions, attacks into enemy ground; the answer is the one who makes them.
explanation.definitionFit: One who makes sudden incursions or attacks into enemy territory is a marauder.

clue.text: Wave to the husky charmer!

parts.note: bran is the husk of grain, the husky part
a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: Wave goodbye to the sled dog with the winning ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'husky' looks like a sled dog, but it is the husks of grain, BRAN. 'Dish' is slang for someone good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: To flourish or wave a weapon or object about threateningly or showily.

clue.text: " This most excellent, the air "(Hamlet)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Hamlet's speech to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern about the sky overhead

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says 'this most excellent canopy, the air, look you, this brave o'erhanging firmament'.
explanation.definitionFit: A covering spread overhead, like the sky arching above, is how Hamlet pictures the heavens.

clue.text: Components of a sweet world

parts.note: liquorice sweets come in a mixed box of many kinds, and the proverb says it takes every kind of person to make a world

explanation.surface: The parts that make up a lovely world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet' is a candy: Liquorice Allsorts are a British mixed liquorice sweet, and the saying 'it takes all sorts to make a world' supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorted liquorice confectionery, and every type of person, which the proverb says make up the world.
